excerpt: Hi friends, genuine question. We all see that top notch Mathematicians can use LLM to prove world class results in a relatively short time of period. OK I admit some of the results are not verified yet, but please hear me. Neither do I know how much “brain” is human and how much is the LLM, because we don’t see the prompts. My question is: what do you think about your career in the future? Please hear me out. In the current world, the way you become a Mathematician, is to get good scores, go to schools, take PHD and then professorship. There may be middle steps like postdoctoral or industry experience, but that’s the general way to do it. And the way that schools judge professors, if I understand correctly, is more about how much results you can get —- ofc if you can obtain big grants then the better, but most of you can’t do that, so I assume that it’s more about the papers. You also teach but that’s not as big as the research. For now, there are a lot of smaller problems left to solve, and since world class Mathematicians tend to devote their life to one world class problem, there are plenty of food for everyone. Does the above make sense? This leads me to the question of: if the future of getting proofs is to prompt with an LLM or whatever AI solution, and it is apparent that world class Mathematicians can prove more conjectures or whatever than they ever can dream without LLM, why do schools need mediocre Mathematicians? I’m not trying to belittle you, but I’m trying to figure out career paths for my son, and I need to understand the impact of AI to all career paths. Again, I iterate, if one world class Mathematicians can prompt through many problems in their lifetime, we face two possibilities: 1. LLMs are good at solving problems but not good at asking new questions, so eventually we have few questions to crack, so the world doesn’t really need that many Mathematicians. 2.
